title: Who Builds on Avalanche: The Companies Behind the Chain's RWA Growth
window: October 2026 snapshot; periods vary by source
description: The companies behind Avalanche’s RWA growth: tokenized assets, institutional credit, stablecoins, payments and dedicated chains.

blocks.text: Avalanche is a network of chains

parts.text: Avalanche is a network of chains

blocks.text: Avalanche is a smart contract network built around one idea: any organization can launch its own chain, called an L1, and set its own rules for who validates, who can access it and how fees work. The public C-Chain sits alongside hundreds of these L1s, and assets can move between them.

parts.text: Avalanche is a smart contract network built around one idea: any organization can launch its own chain, called an L1, and set its own rules for who validates, who can access it and how fees work. The public C-Chain sits alongside hundreds of these L1s, and assets can move between them.

blocks.text: That design is why so many institutions use it. A bank, an exchange or a government agency can run a permissioned chain it controls and still connect to the public network's liquidity.

blocks.text: As the Tokenization Lead at Ava Labs Olivia Vande Woude puts it:

parts.text: As the Tokenization Lead at Ava Labs Olivia Vande Woude puts it:

blocks.text:
“Tokenization puts an asset onchain, but utility is what gives it a market. Assets need to function as collateral, flow into lending markets and move through payment systems. Avalanche already supports 1,255 tokenized RWAs representing more than $13 billion in distributed and represented value, including approximately $484 million in BlackRock’s BUIDL.

The bigger opportunity is putting those assets to work. Avalanche gives institutions customization without isolation. They can build environments around their regulatory and operational requirements while remaining connected to stablecoins, credit markets, applications and buyers across the broader network. Aave’s planned V4 RWA Hub, multi-currency stablecoins and allocators like Grove, with more than $250 million deployed, are building those distribution channels.

This is what invisible adoption looks like. Businesses and consumers gain access to faster payments, productive collateral and deeper credit without needing to think about the blockchain infrastructure underneath.”

blocks.text: Avalanche holds $1.73 billion in distributed RWAs, held in very few wallets

parts.text: Avalanche holds $1.73 billion in distributed RWAs, held in very few wallets

blocks.text: Distributed RWAs on Avalanche stood at $1.73 billion as of October 12, up 2.17% over 30 days, according to rwa.xyz. They are spread across 1,255 assets and 10,058 holder addresses. Represented assets reach $11.40 billion, but one copper-gold token, AZX1, accounts for $10.7 billion of that from a single wallet, as Bitquery has documented.

blocks.text: Governments use Avalanche for records, not securities

parts.text: Governments use Avalanche for records, not securities

blocks.text: Some of the largest deployments on Avalanche never show up in RWA data. California's DMV put 42 million car titles on its own Avalanche chain. The UAE is moving the UAEPASS Digital Vault, used by 12.5 million people, to a dedicated L1. Wyoming launched FRNT, the first U.S. state-issued stablecoin, which can be spent on Avalanche through a Visa card. These are public records and public money rather than investable assets, which is why they sit outside the market cap figures.

blocks.text: Conclusion

parts.text: Conclusion

blocks.text: Avalanche's RWA growth is concentrated. A few issuers, led by Securitize, BlackRock, Circle and Tether, account for most of the value, and their products sit in a small number of wallets.

parts.text: Avalanche's RWA growth is concentrated. A few issuers, led by Securitize, BlackRock, Circle and Tether, account for most of the value, and their products sit in a small number of wallets.

blocks.text: The builders differ more than the numbers suggest. Some issue funds, some lend against them, some move dollars and some run their own chains. What they share is the ability to set their own rules while staying connected to the public network.
